title: Review: Resistivity; Electrical power and energy; Series and parallel circuits; Kirchhoff's laws; EMF and internal resistance
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL08-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL08-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; EL08-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; EL04-uk1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL06-1#N.11, EL04-uk1#N.12, EL05-1#N.11a, EL06-1#N.2, EL06-uk1#N.9, EL08-1#N.10, EL04-uk1#N.3, EL05-1#N.5, EL06-1#N.7, EL06-uk1#N.5, EL08-1#N.3, EL04-uk1#N.11. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: emf
items.clue: Energy transferred to each coulomb of charge by the source.

items.label: Short circuit
items.clue: Connection with R = 0, giving a very large current that heats the cell.

items.label: Internal resistance
items.clue: Property r of a real cell, treated as sitting in series with an ideal cell.

items.label: Micrometer
items.clue: Instrument for finding how wide the wire is at several places; check it for zero error.

questions.stem: Three identical lamps are connected to a supply of negligible internal resistance: lamp A is in series with lamps B and C, which are in parallel with each other. The filament of lamp C breaks. What happens to the brightness of lamps A and B? (Assume each lamp's resistance stays the same.)

options.text: A and B both go out, because the circuit is now broken.
A becomes dimmer and B becomes brighter.
A stays the same and B becomes brighter, because B now carries C's current.
A becomes brighter and B stays the same, because the parallel branch keeps its potential difference.

questions.stem: An unlabelled wire has a mean diameter of 0.32 mm. Its resistance between the clips is 1.72 Ω at a length of 0.20 m and 5.37 Ω at 0.80 m. Resistivities: copper 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m; iron 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m; constantan 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m; nichrome 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m. Which metal is the wire most likely made of?
A 60 W lamp and a 100 W lamp are both rated for a 230 V supply. They are connected in series across a 230 V supply. Assume each keeps its normal working resistance. Which lamp is brighter?

options.text: The 60 W lamp: it has the larger resistance, and in series both carry the same current.
The 100 W lamp: it has the higher power rating, so it gives more light.
The 100 W lamp: a smaller resistance gives more power, as P = V²/R.
Both are equally bright, as they carry the same current.

questions.explanation: R = V²/P: about 880 Ω for the 60 W lamp, 530 Ω for the 100 W lamp. Same current in series, so P = I²R is larger in the 60 W lamp (about 23 W against 14 W).

questions.stem: Three circuits are each made from an identical cell of negligible internal resistance, a resistor and a lamp. In circuit 1 the three form a single closed loop. Circuit 2 is the same loop with an open switch added. Circuit 3 is the same loop as circuit 1 with a wire of negligible resistance connected directly across the lamp's terminals. Which ranks the currents I₁, I₂ and I₃ in the lamps of circuits 1, 2 and 3?

A 15 V supply charges a 12 V battery. They are connected in a single loop, positive terminal to positive terminal, and the total resistance in the loop is 2.0 Ω. What is the current, and which way does it pass through the battery?

options.text: 13.5 A, in at the battery's negative terminal and out at its positive terminal
7.5 A, in at the battery's positive terminal and out at its negative terminal
1.5 A, in at the battery's positive terminal and out at its negative terminal
1.5 A, in at the battery's negative terminal and out at its positive terminal

questions.explanation: Right. Net emf = 15 − 12 = 3.0 V, so I = 1.5 A. The larger emf wins and drives current backwards through the battery: that is charging.

questions.stem: A battery of internal resistance r is connected to an external resistor whose resistance equals r. The external resistor is then replaced by one of resistance 2r. How does the potential difference across the terminals of the battery change?

options.text: It stays equal to its first value.
It rises to 2 times its first value.
It falls to 2/3 of its first value.
It increases to 4/3 of its first value.

questions.stem: A student plots R against length for a uniform wire of diameter 0.40 mm. The best-fit line has a gradient of 4.0 Ω m⁻¹ and crosses the R axis at 0.30 Ω. What is the resistivity of the wire?
questions.explanation: A = π(0.40 × 10⁻³)²/4 = 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m². ρ = gradient × A = 4.0 × 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. The 0.30 Ω intercept (contact resistance) does not affect the gradient.

questions.stem: A steady current of 0.25 A flows in a 24 Ω resistor for 2.0 minutes. How much energy is dissipated in the resistor?
questions.explanation: Power = I²R = 0.25² × 24 = 1.5 W. Energy = power × time = 1.5 W × 120 s = 180 J.

questions.stem: Resistors of 3.0 Ω, 6.0 Ω and 8.0 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance of the combination?

A 9.0 V cell and a 3.0 V cell, both of negligible internal resistance, are connected in a single loop with their emfs opposing each other. The total resistance in the loop is 4.0 Ω. What is the current?

A battery with an internal resistance of 0.50 Ω drives a current of 0.60 A through a lamp, and an ideal voltmeter across the battery's terminals reads 4.2 V. The lamp is then disconnected, so that only the voltmeter remains connected across the battery. What does the voltmeter now read?
questions.explanation: emf = terminal potential difference + Ir = 4.2 + 0.60 × 0.50 = 4.5 V. With no current, the voltmeter reads the emf.

questions.stem: A copper wire and a sample of pure silicon, a semiconductor, are both cooled from 20 °C to −20 °C. How does the resistance of each change, and why?

options.text: Copper's falls: less ion vibration. Silicon's rises: fewer charge carriers.
Both fall, as the ions in each vibrate less, so there are fewer collisions.
Copper's falls, as fewer electrons are freed; silicon's rises, as its ions vibrate more.
Both rise, since cooling makes the charge carriers in each move more slowly.

questions.explanation: Right. In copper the carrier number hardly changes, so fewer collisions win. In silicon the carrier number drops sharply, which outweighs the smaller vibration.
